interactions.summary: Jiang accepts two student answers at once: some Christians treat resurrection as proof of divinity, while another student frames the sacrifice as the hardest possible display of divine love, and Jiang says that love-centered answer is close to Dante's own.

A student presses two objections, that proof by resurrection would destroy faith and that Jesus freely chooses sacrifice rather than being passively sacrificed by God, and Jiang explicitly agrees that free choice is the key correction.

A student reads Beatrice's framing question about how just vengeance can deserve just punishment, Jiang glosses it as the scandal of innocent Jesus suffering for guilty humanity, and the reading begins Beatrice's answer by tracing the problem back to Adam's failed will.
interactions.speaker_attribution: student reading with Jiang doctrinal gloss

speaker_notes.note: These segments are quoted Dante read aloud by a student; Jiang's explanatory gloss appears in segment 0311.

claims.claim: Jiang acknowledges that some Christian denominations explain the crucifixion as proof of Jesus's divinity because he can resurrect himself.
A student argues that sacrificing one's son is the most extreme sign of love, so Christ's death shows how much God loves humanity and wants to cleanse it of sin.
Jiang says the love-centered explanation is close to Dante's own and immediately reframes sacrifice as a willing showing rather than a simple statement that Jesus permanently dies.
A student argues that resurrection cannot function as the basis of faith because once divinity is empirically seen it becomes fact rather than faith.
The same student argues that because Jesus is both human and divine, free will means he chooses sacrifice himself and God cannot simply take that gift away.
Jiang agrees that Jesus sacrifices himself by choice and preserves the claim that Jesus and God are one, so the logic of sacrifice has to pass through willing identity rather than coercion.
Beatrice frames the theological problem as how just vengeance can deserve just punishment.
Jiang glosses that line to mean that God is justly angry at humanity for the fall, yet it remains hard to see why innocent Jesus must suffer in order to answer that anger.
Beatrice begins her answer by saying Adam failed to endure the curb on his will, damned himself, and thereby damned all his descendants.

signature_moments.moment: The student flips the proof argument on its head: if resurrection makes divinity visible as fact, then it cannot be what faith is for.
signature_moments.source_phrase: that's not faith anymore is it
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's sharpest conceptual objection and forces the lecture to treat faith and proof as opposites rather than allies.

signature_moments.moment: Free will reappears as a hard theological limit: God cannot simply cancel the freedom that makes Jesus's sacrifice meaningful.
signature_moments.source_phrase: god cannot take away that gift
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It binds the atonement discussion back to Jiang's larger lecture theme that love and redemption fail if they bypass chosen agency.

signature_moments.moment: Beatrice condenses the whole scandal of Christianity into one paradox: just vengeance somehow becoming just punishment.
signature_moments.source_phrase: how just vengeance can deserve just punishment
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the poem's atonement problem its most compressed formulation and sets up the next sequence of explanation.

signature_moments.moment: The answer begins not with Rome or ritual but with Adam's will failing at the very first curb placed on it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: he could not endure the helpful curb on his willpower
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It roots the punishment problem in freedom and inheritance, not in arbitrary divine anger alone.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Beatrice's name for God's rightful anger at human betrayal, which Jiang treats as the first half of the atonement paradox.
The problem of why Christ's innocent suffering could count as a fitting answer to God's just vengeance against humanity.

glossary_terms.term: the man who was not born
glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Beatrice's circumlocution for Adam, whose misuse of will is said to damn all his progeny.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture moves from student hypotheses about why Christ dies into Beatrice's formal question and then immediately back to Adam, making the crucifixion intelligible only through the older chronology of the fall.
